description: The one brand vocabulary, shared by the card reader (collectai_recognizer/evidence.py) and the logo reader (logos.py). It is a seed, not a limit: every brand name in the catalog index is added to it at scan time, so a brand entered on the Add-a-car form is recognised from the next index export with nothing edited here. This file is for the makers the catalog has not got yet. Add one when you meet one — and run recognizer/tests/test_brands.py, which refuses a name that reads off ordinary card text.
notes: `name` is what gets reported, spelled the way the catalog spells it, because that is what the Add-a-car form prefills and what the matcher compares against a casting's brands.

`spellings` are what the text might read as, lower case; punctuation and spaces are ignored on both sides, so 'Mini GT' and 'minigt' are the same spelling. Add a misreading only if it is one a real logo produces — a loose spelling costs precision across every photo.

A spelling of fewer than 8 characters (BBR, TLV, Siku) is only ever matched as whole words, never inside a longer string. Without that rule a five-letter name finds a five-letter window inside seventy characters of OCR noise, which is how Herpa and Norev came to be reported off photographs of Hot Wheels cards.

This whole list is used for text set in plain type, at 0.86. Logos are matched against the catalog's own brands instead — a garbled wordmark resolves by elimination, and against a list this long it lands anywhere. See brands.on_artwork().

Lines are not brands. Tomica Limited Vintage and TLV Neo are Tomica's lines and the catalog files their cars under Tomica, so they report Tomica; the line belongs in the series field. Same for Kaido House under Mini GT, and Hobby64 and Global64 under Tarmac Works.

Names that read off ordinary card text are deliberately absent, and the test says which: OneModel collided with 'New Models', Neo Models with the same, Trax with 'Turbo Trax', Premium X with 'Premium Bundle', Star Race with 'Easter Raceway'. Tiny is here only as 'toyeast', because 'tiny' is an ordinary word.
